description: Retrieval evaluation set for salt-fat-acid-heat.pdf. Each question is paraphrased (not copied from the book) so retrieval is tested on meaning, not matching words. 'pages' are PDF page numbers (as shown by rag-demo extract), not the printed book's page numbers; a question counts as a hit if a retrieved chunk comes from any listed page. Drafted by Claude from the extracted text; review before relying on it.

questions.question: Why does the author advise against cooking with iodised table salt?
questions.answer: It makes everything taste slightly metallic.

questions.question: How much salt should go in the water for boiling pasta or blanching vegetables?
questions.answer: Enough to make it as salty as the sea (or your memory of it).

questions.question: Is it true that salting the cooking water makes dried beans tough?
questions.answer: No: salt does not toughen dried beans; the usual cause of tough beans is undercooking.

questions.question: At what point should mushrooms be salted so they keep their texture?
questions.answer: Wait until they have just begun to brown in the pan.

questions.question: Which cooking oils work well when you don't want the fat to add any flavour?
questions.answer: Neutral seed or nut oils such as peanut, expeller-pressed canola, or grapeseed, which also have high smoke points.

questions.question: At what temperature does butter go from solid to melted?
questions.answer: It stays solid from 0°C until it melts at 32°C.

questions.question: What is the chemical reaction that browns meat and baked goods called?
questions.answer: The Maillard reaction, named after Louis-Camille Maillard.

questions.question: Why does meat keep cooking after it comes off the heat?
questions.answer: Carryover cooking: residual heat trapped in the food keeps the reactions going.

questions.question: How long should the turkey breast be left in its brine?
questions.answer: Refrigerate overnight, or up to 24 hours.
